rows.searchedFor: can I do some paid freelance work outside my job here?
rows.answer:
A few hours a month on a paid side gig is acceptable, and side gigs should by default be something you work on in your personal time and should not impact the work you do at PostHog.[1]

- The handbook calls them "side gigs" because PostHog is ok with you earning money on the side, but not with this being your main focus and PostHog being just a paycheck.[2]
- The key distinction for a side gig being appropriate is its impact on your work and the amount of time involved.[3]
- Side gigs, whether paid or unpaid, are fine if you are going above and beyond for PostHog and still able to look after yourself properly; the handbook says that isn't possible beyond a certain level of time/energy commitment, but it is happy for you to spend a little time on them each week.[4]
- If you may want the side gig to become your full-time work one day, that is ok; the handbook asks you to let them know so they can create a plan.[5]

rows.searchedFor: Do I need to run paid freelance work outside my job at PostHog by anyone first?
rows.answer:
Yes, the handbook asks you to check in with the relevant Exec team member for your team (James, Tim, or Charles) and get their confirmation before going ahead with any side gig.[1] If your side gig existed before you joined PostHog, this will usually be covered as part of the onboarding process.[2]

A few related points on paid side gigs:
- A few hours a month on a paid side gig is acceptable, and side gigs should by default be done in your personal time without impacting your PostHog work.[3]
- If you want to take an idea that started at PostHog and develop it as an external side project, you need explicit sign-off first.[4]

rows.searchedFor: a big prospect wants a feature promised by Q3 written into their contract - is that ok?
rows.answer:
No. The handbook says PostHog doesn't contract deliverables, and especially doesn't contract to provide deliverables by a certain date, because on principle a single customer would then be forcing it to build something.[1]

- If PostHog has to walk away from a deal because it would have to compromise on these principles, it will, and it can do this because it has a really strong growth engine with its ICP customers.[2]
- PostHog will build things for a big customer as long as it is confident they won't be the only user of that thing, and re-shuffling the roadmap a bit could make sense, but adding things others wouldn't use doesn't.[3]
- Customers need to try PostHog before they expect changes, and the handbook says feedback is welcome but big requirement documents from people who haven't used the product aren't.[4]

rows.searchedFor: how does a YC founder get a desk at Hogpatch?
rows.answer:
A YC founder can't apply for Hogpatch: it's invite-only and isn't open to the whole batch, and when space opens up, PostHog handpicks a few YC companies to join.[1] There is a waitlist, but you can't apply, since founders are handpicked when there's room.[2]

Once invited:
- Judy, the office manager, sends you and your cofounders a digital wallet pass, which gives 24/7 self-service access to the space.[3]
- There's no booking system for desks and phone booths; you just grab a spot when you arrive.[4]
- Each invite lasts 3 months.[5]

rows.searchedFor: why did US customers lose their older Logs data in February?
rows.answer:
A routine mutation to materialize an index finished on Feb 19 and triggered a bug in ClickHouse's zero-copy replication, which caused one replica to erroneously believe all of the data parts in the database were no longer referenced.[1] The replicas then spent roughly 11:02 to 19:40 deleting all of the data stored in S3 for the entire database.[2]

Why it went unnoticed and what was lost:
- Data is only moved to S3 after 24 hours and most queries are for recent data, so the volume of query errors was low and no automated alarms were triggered.[2]
- There was no specific monitoring for the integrity of "cold" data in S3, and the deletion happened silently in the background without application-level errors, so dashboards stayed "green" until a node restart forced a consistency check.[3]
- At 19:40 a node crashed and restarted, and it failed to start because of the large volume of missing data; engineers then found that the vast majority of S3-backed data was missing.[4]
- The result was loss of data collected more than 3 days ago in the US region, affecting only the Logs product.[5]

Kafka's 3 days of retention saved recent activity from total loss.[6]

rows.searchedFor: Did PostHog recover any of the older Logs data that US customers lost in February?
rows.answer:
- The February 19th incident caused the loss of Logs data collected more than 3 days ago in the US region.[1]
- Engineers determined the data was most likely unrecoverable, and disaster recovery procedures started.[2]
- The team decided to cut over to a new table and restore data from Kafka, which has 3 days of retention.[3] The backfill from Kafka history began on Feb 20 at 10:05 and completed at 12:21.[4]
- The handbook says the 3-day Kafka retention saved the team from total data loss for recent activity.[5]

rows.searchedFor: we're launching a beta soon - when do we need to start tracking which users are interested in our product?
rows.answer:
The handbook says you should start tracking product intents as soon as your product is in any sort of public beta, so that data is collected for later when a good activation metric is determined[1]. It also says collecting product intents should be a precursor to any sort of public release[2], so set it up before your beta goes public.

If you mean tracking interest through sign-ups, the handbook says adding items to the coming soon menu early lets you gauge interest in a new feature via sign-ups[3]. It adds that users who registered interest during the Concept stage can opt in to enable the feature once you move it to beta[4].

rows.searchedFor: which of my accounts are big enough to be worth visiting in person?
rows.answer:
The handbook gives two thresholds, and which applies depends on the context.

- In-person visits work best for accounts paying or likely to pay $50k+/year where you've identified specific opportunities for expansion, are navigating renewal conversations, or need to overcome significant technical or organizational hurdles.[1]
- Generally you should be trying to regularly see customers in your book of business who are $100k+ annually, or could get there.[2]
- On how often to go, you should be matching the cadence for in-person meetings with the size of contract (ie. more regular for Very Large, less regular for Large).[3]

rows.searchedFor: how do I pull the posthog org IDs for all my accounts out of salesforce?
rows.answer:
Query PostHog's data warehouse to pull Salesforce data and create a CSV of all PostHog organization IDs for accounts you own.[1] The handbook gives this SQL query for it:

- SELECT DISTINCT posthog_org_id_c, NULL as empty_column FROM salesforce.account WHERE owner_id = 'your_salesforce_id'[2]
- You can find your Salesforce ID by going to your profile and copying the text in the website URL after "/User/".[2]
- Then export the results via CSV.[2]
- The empty column is there so there are commas as delimiters for the org IDs, which lets you copy and paste all the org IDs directly into a filter input text field.[2]

rows.searchedFor: how can I see what posthog is doing on a customer's live site?
rows.answer:
The handbook describes one way to see how PostHog is configured on a customer's site, which is checking whether a reverse proxy is set up. If the customer isn't using session replay, you can add ?__posthog_debug=true to a URL where PostHog is being called, pull up the console logs, type posthog.config and look for the api_host property.[1]

If the customer is using session replay, the handbook gives another route:
- Go to the appropriate replay video, select Activity > Inspector > Doctor, and search for "config".[2]
- Look for PostHog Config, expand the api_host, and see whether the URL is one of PostHog's domains (us.i.posthog.com or eu.i.posthog.com) or one of the customer's own.[2]

If neither method is available because the customer isn't using session replay and the hosted site isn't publicly accessible, you can ask the customer on the discovery call.[3]

rows.searchedFor: How can I check if a customer has set up a reverse proxy for PostHog on their live site?
rows.answer:
The handbook says to check whether the customer has a reverse proxy by looking at their api_host configuration[1], and if it shows us.i.posthog or eu.i.posthog, they are not using a reverse proxy.[2] There are two ways to find it:

- If the customer uses session replay, open the replay video, select Activity > Inspector > Doctor, and search for "config". Find PostHog Config, expand api_host, and see whether the URL is one of PostHog's domains (us.i.posthog.com or eu.i.posthog.com) or one of the customer's own.[3]
- If they aren't using session replay, add ?__posthog_debug=true to a URL where PostHog is being called, open the console logs, type posthog.config, and look for the api_host property.[4]

If neither method is available because the customer doesn't use session replay and the hosted site isn't publicly accessible, you can ask the customer on the discovery call.[5]

Another signal: with either PostHog's managed reverse proxy or a non-managed one, events should populate the "Library custom API host" property, and you should verify the setup with the customer.[6]

rows.searchedFor: what's the street address for Hogpatch? I'm in SF next week
rows.answer:
The handbook says Hogpatch is behind a discreet door off 3rd Street, and the exact location is listed on your digital wallet pass.[1] That wallet pass is described for invited YC founders, so it may not apply to you as a teammate.

For your visit, the handbook says:
- PostHog teammates don't need an invite to use Hogpatch, and if you know your SF travel dates in advance, it's helpful to post in the #sf-bay-area channel so the space can be ready for you.[2]
- If you are visiting for the first time, ring the black intercom doorbell on the front door.[3]
- There's no check-in or reservations needed.[4]
- The Office Manager is on site Mondays to Thursdays from 9am–5pm, and outside those hours you can reach out in the #project-hogpatch channel or DM her directly.[5]

rows.answer:

- The post-departure exercise window is 10 years, and most team members who leave will be deemed a 'good leaver' unless they have been terminated due to gross misconduct.[1]
